chapters.title: Choose the system and account for energy
points: Heat absorbed is positive; expansion work on the system is negative.
Absorb 500 J and do 200 J of work: ΔU = +300 J.
chapters.script: Welcome to Chemical Thermodynamics. This recorded Chemistry class uses an AI generated Marin voice. Begin every energy calculation by choosing the system. An open system exchanges matter and energy with its surroundings. A closed system exchanges energy but not matter. An isolated system exchanges neither. Internal energy, enthalpy and entropy are state functions: their changes depend on initial and final states. Heat and work describe energy transfer along a path. Temperature and pressure are intensive properties; total volume and total internal energy are extensive. In the Chemistry convention, the first law is change in internal energy equals heat plus work done on the system. Heat entering is positive. Compression work is positive, while expansion work is negative. For expansion against a constant external pressure, work is minus external pressure times the volume increase. Consider a closed system that absorbs five hundred joules and expands by one litre against two bar. One litre bar equals one hundred joules. The work is therefore minus two hundred joules, and the internal energy increases by three hundred joules. The system gained heat but returned some energy to the surroundings as work. Notice that external pressure appears in this work expression. If it varies, the appropriate pressure volume integral is needed. Free expansion against zero external pressure does no pressure volume work. Adiabatic means no heat transfer; it does not automatically mean constant temperature. Isothermal means constant temperature. Isochoric means constant volume, and isobaric means constant pressure. For an ideal gas, internal energy depends only on temperature, so an isothermal change has zero internal energy change even though heat and work may each be nonzero. Keep the signs tied to the chosen system, and always convert litre bar into energy units before adding heat and work.

chapters.title: Connect enthalpy, heat and gas stoichiometry
chapters.formula: H = U + PV; ΔH = ΔU + Δng RT
points: At constant pressure, qp = ΔH for a closed system with only PV work.
N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃: Δng = 2 − 4 = −2.
At 300 K and ΔU = −90.0 kJ: ΔH ≈ −95.0 kJ.
chapters.script: Enthalpy is defined as internal energy plus pressure times volume. For a closed system undergoing only pressure volume work at constant pressure, the heat transferred equals the enthalpy change. At constant volume, with no other work, heat equals the internal energy change. The conditions are part of the result. An exothermic process has a negative enthalpy change, while an endothermic process has a positive one. For ideal gaseous reactants and products at the same temperature, the gas contribution gives change in enthalpy equals change in internal energy plus change in gaseous mole number times R T. In ordinary reaction calculations this form neglects condensed phase pressure volume contributions. Count only gaseous species when finding the gaseous mole change. For one nitrogen plus three hydrogen forming two ammonia, all gases, the change is two minus four, or minus two moles per reaction as written. Suppose the internal energy change is minus ninety point zero kilojoules for that reaction amount at three hundred kelvin. Use R equal to zero point zero zero eight three one four kilojoules per mole kelvin. The correction is minus two times R times three hundred, about minus four point nine nine kilojoules. The enthalpy change is about minus ninety five point zero kilojoules. Reversing the reaction reverses both energy changes and the gaseous mole change. A separate useful relation for one mole of an ideal gas is molar heat capacity at constant pressure minus molar heat capacity at constant volume equals R. It is not a universal identity for liquids, solids or real gases. Heat capacity relates heat to temperature change under specified conditions; if it varies appreciably with temperature, use an integral instead of a constant value. Check the phase labels and the reaction amount before substituting numbers.

chapters.title: Build Hess cycles and interpret enthalpy data
points: Reverse a reaction → reverse its enthalpy sign.
C + O₂ → CO₂: −394; reverse CO oxidation: +283 kJ.
Adding gives C + ½O₂ → CO: ΔH = −111 kJ.
chapters.script: Hess's law follows from enthalpy being a state function. A reaction may be assembled from several steps; adding their enthalpy changes gives the same overall change. Reverse a step and reverse its sign. Multiply an equation by a number and multiply its enthalpy by that number. Here is an illustrative cycle. Carbon as graphite plus oxygen forming carbon dioxide has enthalpy minus three hundred ninety four kilojoules per mole of reaction. Carbon monoxide plus half an oxygen forming carbon dioxide has enthalpy minus two hundred eighty three. We want graphite plus half an oxygen forming carbon monoxide. Keep the first equation and reverse the second. Carbon dioxide cancels, leaving the target reaction. Add minus three hundred ninety four to plus two hundred eighty three to obtain minus one hundred eleven kilojoules. These rounded values illustrate the calculation; phases and reference conditions must match. Standard formation enthalpy refers to forming one mole of a substance from its elements in their reference states. The standard formation enthalpy of an element in its reference state is assigned zero; this does not say that its internal energy or entropy is zero. Multiply each formation enthalpy by its stoichiometric coefficient, then subtract the reactant sum from the product sum. Combustion enthalpy concerns complete burning of the specified amount, usually one mole, with product phases stated. Atomization creates gaseous atoms. Sublimation converts solid to gas. Ionization removes an electron from a gaseous species, while hydration brings gaseous ions into water. Dissolution can combine lattice separation and solvation effects. For a gas phase bond estimate, add energies of bonds broken and subtract energies of bonds formed. Average bond enthalpies give an approximation because bond environments differ. Do not mix an average gas bond estimate with a liquid phase reaction without accounting for phase changes.

chapters.title: Use entropy and temperature to predict direction
points: Spontaneous change: ΔSuniverse > 0; system entropy alone is insufficient.
ΔH = −40 kJ; ΔS = −0.100 kJ/K → Tcross = 400 K.
At 300 K: ΔG = −10 kJ; at 500 K: ΔG = +10 kJ.
chapters.script: Energy conservation alone does not choose the direction of a process. Entropy supplies the second law criterion: a spontaneous change increases the total entropy of the system and surroundings. The system's entropy may decrease if the surroundings gain more. A reversible ideal limit has zero total entropy production. For a reversible isothermal path, entropy change is reversible heat divided by temperature. More generally, integrate reversible heat divided by temperature along a suitable path between the states. Entropy is a state function, even when the actual path is irreversible. For the usual closed system at constant temperature and pressure, without imposed non pressure volume work, a negative Gibbs energy change identifies a thermodynamically favourable direction. Gibbs energy change is enthalpy change minus temperature times entropy change. Temperature must be in kelvin. Match the energy units before subtracting. Suppose enthalpy change is minus forty kilojoules and entropy change is minus one hundred joules per kelvin. Convert the entropy to minus zero point one zero zero kilojoules per kelvin. At three hundred kelvin, Gibbs energy change is minus forty plus thirty, or minus ten kilojoules. At five hundred kelvin, it is minus forty plus fifty, or plus ten. If both enthalpy and entropy changes are approximately temperature independent over the range, the crossover is four hundred kelvin. This exothermic process with decreasing entropy is favoured at lower temperature. Positive enthalpy and positive entropy favour higher temperature. Negative enthalpy and positive entropy favour the forward direction throughout the temperature range where those signs hold. The opposite pair does not. Finally, favourable does not mean fast. A large activation barrier can make a thermodynamically favourable reaction very slow. Keep the direction question separate from the kinetics question.

chapters.title: Distinguish standard Gibbs energy and equilibrium
chapters.formula: ΔG = ΔG° + RT ln Q; ΔG° = −RT ln K
points: Q describes the current mixture; K describes equilibrium at that temperature.
At 300 K, ΔG° ≈ −5.744 kJ/mol gives K ≈ 10.
Q < K: forward favoured; Q > K: reverse favoured.
chapters.script: The standard Gibbs energy change and the Gibbs energy change for the current mixture are different quantities. The connection is Gibbs energy change equals standard Gibbs energy change plus R T times the natural logarithm of the reaction quotient Q. The rigorous quotient uses dimensionless activities relative to standard states. For ideal dilute solutions and ideal gases, concentration or pressure ratios provide useful approximations. At equilibrium, the reaction Gibbs energy change is zero and Q equals the equilibrium constant K. Substitution gives standard Gibbs energy change equals minus R T times the natural logarithm of K. Thus a negative standard Gibbs energy change implies K greater than one at that temperature. It does not guarantee that every possible mixture will proceed forward. Take standard Gibbs energy change approximately minus five point seven four four kilojoules per mole at three hundred kelvin. With R equal to zero point zero zero eight three one four kilojoules per mole kelvin, the natural logarithm of K is about two point three zero three. K is approximately ten. If Q is one, the forward direction is favoured. If Q is one hundred, Gibbs energy change is positive, about plus five point seven four kilojoules per mole, and the reverse direction is favoured. If Q is ten, the mixture is at equilibrium. Combining the equations gives Gibbs energy change equals R T times the natural logarithm of Q divided by K. This directly connects composition to direction. Standard conditions do not automatically mean two hundred ninety eight kelvin; always read the stated temperature. Finish with a short checklist: define the system, choose the correct work sign, preserve reaction coefficients and phases, convert entropy units, and distinguish Q from K. Use the worked notes and six original practice questions. This is the core Unit four foundation; detailed enthalpy cycles, entropy integrals and wider mixed problems remain for further study.

chapters.title: Formation and bond-enthalpy calculations
chapters.script: Formation enthalpies let us assemble a reaction without measuring it directly. Use the balanced coefficients and the physical states in the data. For methane combustion to carbon dioxide gas and liquid water, take illustrative standard formation enthalpies in kilojoules per mole: methane minus seventy five, carbon dioxide minus three hundred ninety four, and liquid water minus two hundred eighty six. Oxygen in its reference state contributes zero. Products contribute minus three hundred ninety four plus twice minus two hundred eighty six, giving minus nine hundred sixty six. Subtract the reactant contribution of minus seventy five. The reaction enthalpy is minus eight hundred ninety one kilojoules per mole of methane for these rounded data. Changing the product to water vapour changes the answer. Average bond enthalpies instead estimate energy for gas phase bonds broken minus bonds formed. They are approximate and do not automatically include condensation or solid lattice effects. An element's zero standard formation enthalpy applies to its reference state, not to every allotrope, gaseous atom or ion. Always label the amount and phase beside a thermochemical result.
points: Reactants · −75 + 2(0) · −75
Products − reactants · −966 − (−75) · −891 kJ mol⁻¹

chapters.title: Lattice dissociation and hydration
chapters.script: An ionic dissolution cycle separates processes that are easily confused. First imagine pulling the solid into separated gaseous ions. Define this lattice dissociation enthalpy as positive. Then hydrate those gaseous ions to the chosen aqueous reference states; hydration enthalpies are normally negative. Adding both stages gives the enthalpy of solution for matching endpoints and concentration conventions. With illustrative values of plus seven hundred eighty kilojoules per mole for lattice dissociation and minus seven hundred fifty for total hydration, dissolution has enthalpy plus thirty kilojoules per mole. A positive result does not by itself prove that dissolution is impossible, because the Gibbs energy also contains an entropy contribution. Some tables instead define lattice enthalpy for forming the solid from gaseous ions. That is the opposite process and has the opposite sign. Never insert a number until its process is clear. Atomization, ionization and electron attachment provide further steps in a full Born Haber cycle. Keep each species and charge balanced when adding them. This two stage example isolates dissolution bookkeeping rather than claiming to reproduce every step of a complete formation cycle.

Total hydration · −750 · Gas ions → aqueous ions
Dissolution · +30 · Sum matching endpoints

chapters.title: Calorimetry with the vessel included
chapters.script: A calorimeter records a temperature change in material surrounding the reacting system. Include every heat capacity specified in the problem. Suppose one hundred grams of solution has specific heat capacity four point two joules per gram kelvin, and the calorimeter contributes eighty joules per kelvin. The combined heat capacity is four hundred twenty plus eighty, or five hundred joules per kelvin. A temperature rise of two kelvin means the measured surroundings gain one thousand joules. If heat loss is negligible, the reaction releases one thousand joules. For zero point zero five zero mole reacting as written, the molar heat is minus twenty kilojoules per mole. The negative sign belongs to the reaction, while the solution and vessel gained heat. At approximately constant pressure with only pressure volume work, the reaction heat corresponds to enthalpy change. In a rigid bomb calorimeter, the corresponding constant volume heat gives internal energy change; convert to enthalpy when the gas mole correction is required. Check whether a supplied calorimeter constant already includes the solution before adding its heat capacity again.
points: Total heat capacity · 100 × 4.2 + 80 · 500 J K⁻¹
Surroundings heat · 500 × 2 · +1000 J
Per mole reaction · −1.00 / 0.050 · −20 kJ mol⁻¹

chapters.title: Entropy from a reversible reference path
chapters.script: Entropy change must be evaluated using a reversible reference path between the same endpoints. Heat divided by temperature is not a universal expression for an arbitrary irreversible transfer. At an equilibrium phase transition at constant temperature and pressure, the molar entropy change is the molar transition enthalpy divided by that temperature. For melting with illustrative enthalpy six kilojoules per mole at three hundred kelvin, the entropy increase is twenty joules per mole kelvin. Freezing between the reverse endpoints gives minus twenty. For warming a substance at constant pressure with approximately constant molar heat capacity, integrate heat capacity divided by temperature. The result is molar heat capacity times the natural logarithm of final temperature divided by initial temperature. With thirty joules per mole kelvin and warming from three hundred to six hundred kelvin, the increase is thirty times the natural logarithm of two, about twenty point eight joules per mole kelvin. Both temperatures must be absolute. If heat capacity varies appreciably, retain it inside the integral rather than reusing the constant value shortcut.
points: Melting at equilibrium · 6000 / 300 · +20.0
Reverse freezing · −6000 / 300 · −20.0
Constant Cp warming · 30 ln(600/300) · +20.8

board.heading: Entropy from a reversible reference path

chapters.title: System, surroundings and the second law
chapters.script: A system can lose entropy while a spontaneous process increases the total entropy of system and surroundings. Consider an illustrative process at three hundred kelvin and constant pressure that releases six kilojoules per mole into a large thermal reservoir. Assume only pressure volume work and negligible changes elsewhere. The reservoir receives six thousand joules per mole, so its entropy increases by twenty joules per mole kelvin. If the system entropy decreases by ten joules per mole kelvin, the total increases by ten. The process is thermodynamically favourable under those stated conditions. Its Gibbs energy change is minus six kilojoules minus three hundred times minus zero point zero one zero kilojoules per kelvin, giving minus three kilojoules per mole. Negative temperature times the universe entropy change gives the same result under these constraints. The reservoir temperature is effectively constant; do not divide a large varying temperature heat transfer by one arbitrary temperature. This example also shows why exothermic and spontaneous are different labels. Identify the surroundings, constraints and entropy contribution before using the sign of heat as a direction test.
points: Surroundings entropy · +6000 / 300 · +20 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹
Universe entropy · −10 + 20 · +10 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹
System Gibbs change · −6 − 300(−0.010) · −3 kJ mol⁻¹

board.heading: System, surroundings and the second law

chapters.title: Compare reversible and constant-pressure expansion
chapters.script: Work depends on the path even when an ideal gas begins and ends at the same temperature and volumes. Consider one mole at three hundred kelvin expanding from two to four litres. For a reversible isothermal path, work done on the gas in the Chemistry sign convention is minus n R T times the natural logarithm of two. Using R eight point three one four joules per mole kelvin gives about minus one point seven two nine kilojoules. Now compare an isothermal expansion against constant external pressure equal to the final ideal gas pressure. The final pressure is n R T divided by the final volume. Multiplying that pressure by the two litre volume increase gives work about minus one point two four seven kilojoules. Use compatible volume units in both factors. The reversible path supplies a greater magnitude of expansion work between these endpoints. For the ideal gas, internal energy change is zero in both isothermal cases, so heat entering balances the negative work. Reversible does not mean zero work, and isothermal does not mean zero heat. The comparison assumes only pressure volume work, the stated ideal gas model and suitable heat exchange to maintain temperature.
points: Reversible isothermal · −8.314×300×ln 2 · w ≈ −1.729 kJ
Constant Pext = final pressure · −nRT(1 − V₁/V₂) · w ≈ −1.247 kJ
Both ideal-gas isothermal paths · ΔU = 0; q = −w · Heat is path dependent

chapters.title: Adiabatic compression need not be isothermal
chapters.formula: Reversible ideal gas: TV^(γ−1) = constant; q = 0
chapters.script: Adiabatic means no heat transfer, not unchanged temperature. As a supporting ideal gas application, take one mole of a monatomic gas initially at three hundred kelvin. Compress it reversibly and adiabatically to half its initial volume, using constant molar heat capacities and gamma equal to five thirds. The reversible ideal gas relation gives final temperature equal to three hundred times two raised to the two thirds power, or about four hundred seventy six point two kelvin. Internal energy rises by n C V times the temperature increase. With C V equal to three halves R, the rise is about two point one nine eight kilojoules using R eight point three one four. Heat is zero, so work done on the gas is positive by that amount in the Chemistry convention. An irreversible adiabatic change still has zero heat, but it cannot automatically use the same reversible volume temperature relation. Likewise a gas with temperature dependent heat capacities needs a more careful calculation. State reversibility, ideal behaviour and constant heat capacities before applying this power law. The example reinforces first law signs rather than replacing the separate Physics treatment of complete gas cycles.
points: CV = 3R/2 · nCV(T₂ − T₁) · ΔU ≈ +2.198 kJ
Adiabatic: q = 0 · ΔU = q + w · w ≈ +2.198 kJ

chapters.title: Correct a reaction enthalpy for temperature
chapters.formula: Constant ΔCp model: ΔH(T₂) = ΔH(T₁) + ΔCp(T₂−T₁)
chapters.script: A reaction enthalpy quoted at one temperature need not have exactly the same value at another. A Hess cycle can connect the temperatures by warming reactants and products through their respective heat capacities. The reaction heat capacity change is the sum of product heat capacities with stoichiometric coefficients minus the corresponding reactant sum. If that difference is approximately constant over the range and no phase transition intervenes, the enthalpy correction is reaction heat capacity change times the temperature increase. Take a supplied reaction enthalpy minus one hundred kilojoules per mole at two hundred ninety eight kelvin and reaction heat capacity change plus fifty joules per mole kelvin. Raising the temperature to three hundred ninety eight kelvin adds plus five kilojoules per mole, so the corrected reaction enthalpy is minus ninety five. The reaction remains exothermic in this model but is less exothermic at the higher temperature. Convert joules into kilojoules before adding. If heat capacity varies, keep it inside the temperature integral; if a phase transition occurs, include its enthalpy separately. This is a supporting temperature correction derived from state functions, not permission to extrapolate a constant heat capacity indefinitely.

ΔCp = +50 J/(mol K) · 50×(398−298) / 1000 · +5.00 kJ/mol correction

chapters.title: Build reaction entropy from a balanced table
chapters.script: Standard molar entropy values are combined with the balanced reaction coefficients, not simply compared one species at a time. Use the written reaction one nitrogen molecule plus three hydrogen molecules giving two ammonia molecules, all gaseous. Suppose supplied standard molar entropies are one hundred ninety two, one hundred thirty one and one hundred ninety three joules per mole kelvin for nitrogen, hydrogen and ammonia respectively. The product sum is two times one hundred ninety three, or three hundred eighty six. The reactant sum is one hundred ninety two plus three times one hundred thirty one, or five hundred eighty five. Reaction entropy is therefore minus one hundred ninety nine joules per mole of reaction kelvin. All individual entropy values are positive while their reaction difference is negative. If the supplied reaction enthalpy is minus ninety two kilojoules per mole of reaction at two hundred ninety eight kelvin, standard Gibbs energy is about minus thirty two point seven kilojoules after converting the entropy units. The coefficients define the reaction amount throughout. This calculation uses the stated standard states and supplied rounded data, not a claim that every entropy can be inferred solely from counting gas molecules.

Reactant entropy sum · 192 + 3×131 · 585 J/(mol reaction K)

chapters.title: Match constant-volume heat to the written reaction
chapters.formula: For ideal gases: ΔrH = ΔrU + ΔngRT
chapters.script: A constant volume heat measurement and a reaction enthalpy are not automatically the same number. For a closed reaction system with only pressure volume work, constant volume heat gives internal energy change. At constant pressure the corresponding heat gives enthalpy change under the usual conditions. Consider the supplied illustrative reaction data for two hydrogen molecules plus one oxygen molecule forming two liquid water molecules at three hundred kelvin. Let internal energy change be minus five hundred sixty kilojoules per mole of that written reaction. Only gaseous species enter the ideal gas mole correction: there are zero gaseous product moles and three gaseous reactant moles, so the change is minus three. Using R zero point zero zero eight three one four kilojoules per mole kelvin, the enthalpy is minus five hundred sixty minus seven point four eight three, or about minus five hundred sixty seven point four eight kilojoules per mole of reaction. Producing one mole of liquid water corresponds to half the written reaction, so both energy changes must be halved for that basis. Including liquid water in the gas count would give the wrong correction. Preserve phases, coefficients and the stated reaction basis before comparing heat measurements.

chapters.title: Reaction extent scales an extensive heat

chapters.script: A reaction enthalpy belongs to a particular balanced equation. Consider the supplied equation two moles of hydrogen plus one mole of oxygen forming two moles of liquid water, with reaction enthalpy minus five hundred seventy two kilojoules per mole of reaction extent. Start with zero point three zero zero mole hydrogen and zero point one zero zero mole oxygen. Dividing each amount by its stoichiometric coefficient gives possible extents zero point one five zero and zero point one zero zero mole. Oxygen limits the extent to zero point one zero zero mole. The reaction forms zero point two zero zero mole water and leaves zero point one zero zero mole hydrogen. At constant pressure with only pressure volume work, the reaction heat is minus fifty seven point two kilojoules. Writing the equation for one mole water halves its reaction enthalpy but doubles the numerical extent for the same physical conversion. Their product stays unchanged. Distinguish reaction extent from product amount, and keep the written coefficient convention attached to every molar reaction enthalpy.

chapters.title: Phase-change entropy needs the transition temperature
chapters.formula: ΔSₜᵣ = ΔHₜᵣ/Tₜᵣ for a reversible equilibrium transition
chapters.script: At a phase transition carried out reversibly at its equilibrium temperature and pressure, the entropy change is the transition enthalpy divided by the absolute transition temperature. Use supplied illustrative fusion enthalpy six point zero zero kilojoules per mole at three hundred kelvin. Melting two point zero zero moles absorbs twelve point zero kilojoules and raises the system entropy by forty point zero joules per kelvin. A thermal reservoir at the same temperature loses forty point zero joules per kelvin in the reversible limit. The total is zero, consistent with equilibrium rather than a finite thermodynamic driving force. Freezing reverses both signs for the same endpoints. This shortcut uses the transition temperature, not an arbitrary room temperature. Away from phase equilibrium, use an appropriate reversible reference path with heating or cooling stages as needed. A positive entropy change of the sample alone does not establish spontaneity, because the surroundings must also be included. State the phase, amount, pressure and transition temperature before applying the ratio.

board.heading: Phase-change entropy needs the transition temperature

chapters.title: Heat flow generates entropy between reservoirs
chapters.script: Heat transferred across a finite temperature difference produces entropy even when energy is conserved. Suppose an isolated combined model contains ideal reservoirs at four hundred and three hundred kelvin. One thousand joules flows from the hot reservoir to the cold reservoir, with no work and no energy loss elsewhere. The hot reservoir loses two point five zero joules per kelvin of entropy. The cold reservoir gains three point three three joules per kelvin. Their total entropy change is positive zero point eight three three joule per kelvin. The two energy changes cancel, but the entropy changes do not, because equal heat is divided by different temperatures. Reversing only this heat transfer would make the combined entropy change negative and cannot happen spontaneously in the isolated model. A refrigerator can move heat in that direction only with additional processes and an energy supply. The reservoir approximation means each temperature stays essentially constant during the transfer. Finite bodies that noticeably change temperature require integration rather than using these two fixed denominators.

chapters.title: A negative standard Gibbs energy does not fix direction
chapters.formula: ΔᵣG = RT ln(Q/K); use dimensionless activities
chapters.script: Standard reaction Gibbs energy describes standard states, while actual direction also depends on composition. Use the relation reaction Gibbs energy equals R T times the natural logarithm of Q divided by K. For an illustrative reaction at three hundred kelvin, let the dimensionless equilibrium constant be ten and the current dimensionless reaction quotient one hundred. The quotient exceeds the equilibrium constant. Using R equal to eight point three one four joules per mole kelvin gives reaction Gibbs energy plus five point seven four kilojoules per mole of reaction. The forward reaction is thermodynamically uphill at this composition, so the reverse direction is favoured. Yet the standard reaction Gibbs energy is minus R T logarithm ten, or minus five point seven four kilojoules per mole. There is no contradiction: the two values refer to different conditions. At Q equal to K, actual reaction Gibbs energy is zero. Activities are dimensionless; concentration ratios approximate them only under suitable assumptions. Thermodynamic preference does not specify how quickly equilibrium is approached.

chapters.title: Close a complete Born–Haber cycle

chapters.script: A Born Haber cycle makes every intermediate in an ionic formation calculation explicit. Start with one mole of solid sodium and half a mole of gaseous chlorine, ending with one mole of solid sodium chloride. In a supplied teaching dataset, sodium sublimation costs one hundred eight kilojoules per mole. Its first ionization costs four hundred ninety six. Half the chlorine bond dissociation costs one hundred twenty two, and electron gain by gaseous chlorine releases three hundred forty nine. These signed stages total positive three hundred seventy seven kilojoules before lattice formation. If the standard formation enthalpy is negative four hundred eleven, gaseous ions must release seven hundred eighty eight kilojoules on forming the solid. Reversing that last arrow gives positive seven hundred eighty eight for lattice dissociation. The chlorine bond term is halved because the formation equation uses half a molecule of chlorine per formula unit. Electron gain is entered as a signed enthalpy change here, not as an unsigned affinity magnitude. State the arrow and convention before substituting any value.

chapters.title: Integrate a changing reaction heat capacity
chapters.script: A constant heat capacity correction is a useful approximation, but a supplied temperature dependent function must be integrated. Keep the balanced reaction and its amount basis fixed. Suppose its product minus reactant heat capacity is ten plus zero point zero two zero times temperature, in joules per mole of reaction per kelvin. Take the standard reaction enthalpy at three hundred kelvin as negative fifty point zero kilojoules per mole. Between three hundred and five hundred kelvin, the constant term contributes two thousand joules per mole. The linear term integrates to zero point zero one zero times the difference of the squared temperatures, adding one thousand six hundred joules per mole. The total correction is positive three point six zero kilojoules, making the new enthalpy negative forty six point four zero. Do not insert one endpoint heat capacity into the constant formula and call it an exact integral. This supplied linear model is valid only over its stated interval with unchanged phases. A phase transition or different reaction normalization requires additional accounting rather than silently extending the same polynomial.

chapters.title: Mixing different ideal gases increases entropy
chapters.formula: ΔmixS = −RΣnᵢ ln xᵢ; equal 1 mol samples: 2R ln 2
chapters.script: Consider one mole each of two chemically different ideal gases, initially separated at the same temperature and pressure. Their starting volumes are equal. Removing the partition lets each component spread into twice its initial volume. A reversible reference expansion for each gas gives an entropy increase of the gas constant times the natural logarithm of two. Adding the contributions gives about eleven point five three joules per kelvin for the two mole sample. This is a total entropy change, not a value per mole of mixture. At three hundred kelvin the corresponding ideal mixing Gibbs change is about negative three point four six kilojoules, since ideal mixing at fixed temperature has zero enthalpy change. The spontaneous partition removal itself need not be reversible; entropy is evaluated through a reference path. If both compartments instead contain the same gas at identical temperature and pressure, removing their artificial partition creates no thermodynamic mixing entropy. Do not label identical particles as different chemical components simply to force a positive answer. Real gas interactions or unequal initial conditions require a different calculation.
points: 1 mol A + 1 mol B · Different ideal gases; same T,p · xA = xB = ½
Each expands to twice V · ΔS total = 2R ln 2 · +11.53 J/K
At T = 300 K · ΔHmix = 0; ΔG = −TΔS · −3.46 kJ for sample

chapters.title: Rescaling a reaction changes its standard Gibbs value
chapters.formula: Reaction × a: ΔrG° × a and K → Kᵃ; reversal: K → 1/K
chapters.script: An equilibrium constant belongs to a written reaction at a specified temperature. Standard reaction Gibbs energy is also tied to that stoichiometric normalization. Suppose an original reaction has dimensionless equilibrium constant nine. Doubling every coefficient doubles its standard reaction Gibbs energy, so the new constant is eighty one, not eighteen. Reversing the original reaction changes the sign of its standard Gibbs energy and gives one ninth for its equilibrium constant. Halving the original coefficients instead gives the square root, which is three. These operations follow from standard reaction Gibbs energy equals negative R T times the natural logarithm of K. Multiplying an energy therefore multiplies the logarithm, rather than the constant itself. This bookkeeping does not change the physical equilibrium mixture: the new quotient is transformed by the same power, and it still equals the matching constant at equilibrium. Keep temperature fixed throughout the comparison and use dimensionless thermodynamic activities. Merely changing the initial amounts without changing the written reaction does not rescale its constant. Distinguish equation normalization from changing temperature or from moving a mixture away from equilibrium.
points: Original K = 9 · Double coefficients · ΔrG° doubles; K = 81
Reverse original equation · Change sign of ΔrG° · K = 1/9
Halve original equation · Half the logarithm · K = √9 = 3

chapters.title: Insulated free expansion can generate entropy without heat
chapters.formula: Ideal gas; q=0, w=0, ΔU=0, ΔT=0; ΔS=nR ln(V₂/V₁)>0
chapters.script: Zero heat transfer does not force zero entropy change in an irreversible process. Consider one mole of an ideal gas initially confined to half of a rigid insulated container, with vacuum in the other half. Removing the internal partition doubles the volume available to the gas. External pressure opposing this free expansion is zero, so pressure volume work is zero. The insulated outer walls give zero heat transfer. In the Chemistry convention, internal energy change equals heat plus work and is therefore zero. For an ideal gas, internal energy depends only on temperature, so the final equilibrium temperature equals the initial one. Nevertheless entropy rises. Evaluate it through a reversible isothermal reference path between those same endpoints, giving R times the natural logarithm of two, approximately five point seven six joules per kelvin. This reference path calculates a state function; it is not the actual gas motion inside the vessel. The isolated whole has positive entropy generation while its surroundings exchange no heat. A real gas can show a temperature change in an analogous expansion, and the reversible adiabatic volume temperature power law cannot be imposed on this irreversible event.
points: Rigid insulated container; initial vacuum · q=0; external pressure=0; w=0 · ΔU=0
One mole ideal gas; V₂=2V₁ · ΔT=0; ΔS=R ln2 · ΔS≈+5.76 J/K
Irreversible actual expansion · Use reversible path only to calculate ΔS · Do not use reversible adiabatic power law

chapters.title: Two gas endpoints need both thermal and volume entropy terms
chapters.formula: ΔS=nCv ln(T₂/T₁)+nR ln(V₂/V₁) for an ideal gas with constant Cv
chapters.script: When an ideal gas changes both temperature and volume, keeping just one entropy term misses part of the endpoint change. Construct a reversible reference path consisting of constant volume warming followed by isothermal expansion at the final temperature. For constant molar heat capacity, the warming contribution is n C V times the natural logarithm of final over initial temperature. The expansion contribution is n R times the logarithm of final over initial volume. Add them because entropy is a state function. Take one mole of a monatomic ideal gas with C V equal to three halves R, temperature increasing from three hundred to six hundred kelvin and volume from ten to twenty litres. Each logarithm is the natural logarithm of two, so the sum is five halves R times that logarithm, approximately fourteen point four one joules per kelvin. Reversing both endpoints changes the sign. These endpoints even have the same ideal gas pressure because temperature and volume double together, but that does not make the entropy change zero. The actual process may follow a different path; its heat and work are not fixed by this entropy calculation alone.
points: n=1; Cv=3R/2; 300→600 K · Thermal term=(3R/2) ln2 · Use absolute temperatures
Volume 10→20 L · Volume term=R ln2 · Only the ratio needs matching volume units
Total: (5R/2) ln2 · ΔS≈+14.41 J/K · Same endpoint pressure does not mean ΔS=0

chapters.title: Use a temperature interval to predict a new equilibrium constant
chapters.script: An equilibrium constant belongs to a specified temperature as well as a specified balanced reaction. A supporting integrated van't Hoff calculation predicts its temperature change when reaction enthalpy is approximately constant over the interval. The natural logarithm of K two divided by K one equals minus standard reaction enthalpy divided by R, multiplied by one over temperature two minus one over temperature one. Suppose the supplied reaction has enthalpy plus thirty kilojoules per mole, with K equal to two at three hundred kelvin. At three hundred thirty kelvin, first convert the enthalpy to thirty thousand joules per mole to match R eight point three one four. The logarithm of the constant ratio is approximately one point zero nine three, giving a ratio about two point nine eight five and a new constant about five point nine seven. The increase agrees with the endothermic sign. For a negative reaction enthalpy over the same heating interval, the constant would decrease. Do not replace the natural logarithm with a base ten logarithm without its conversion factor, or hold enthalpy constant across a phase change without checking the model.
points: Positive enthalpy; heating · K increases for this equation · Constant ΔH° approximation; natural log

chapters.title: A neutralization cycle can isolate an ionization enthalpy
chapters.script: Neutralization data can reveal a hidden ionization step if all reactions and states are matched. In a supplied dilute solution Hess model, hydrogen ion plus hydroxide forms water with enthalpy minus fifty seven kilojoules per mole water. A weak acid H A reacting with hydroxide gives A minus and water with enthalpy minus fifty five kilojoules per mole water. Add the formal ionization of H A into hydrogen ion and A minus to the first reaction. Hydrogen ions cancel, leaving the weak acid neutralization equation. Therefore ionization enthalpy plus minus fifty seven equals minus fifty five, and ionization enthalpy is plus two kilojoules per mole. In this dataset the endothermic ionization step offsets some heat released by water formation. This is not a universal numerical value for every weak acid, and weak ionization is not automatically an endothermic process in every case. Compare like amounts of water and compatible dilute solution states before subtracting measurements. Heat absorbed by a calorimeter has the opposite sign to the reaction heat, so an observed temperature rise must first be converted to a consistently signed reaction enthalpy.
points: H⁺+OH⁻→H₂O · ΔH=−57 kJ/mol water · Matched dilute-state baseline
HA+OH⁻→A⁻+H₂O · ΔH=−55 kJ/mol water · Ionization step is included
ΔHion−57=−55 · ΔHion=+2 kJ/mol · Dataset-specific; preserve reaction signs

chapters.title: Isomer combustion cycles compare enthalpies at matched states
chapters.formula: ΔH(A→B)=ΔcH(A)−ΔcH(B), when both combustion endpoints match
chapters.script: Two isomers can have the same molecular formula but different enthalpies. A combustion cycle can measure their difference if the product amounts, product phases and temperature match. Use supplied illustrative molar combustion enthalpies minus three thousand kilojoules for isomer A and minus two thousand nine hundred eighty for isomer B, each leading to the same carbon dioxide and liquid water endpoint. Burn A, then reverse the combustion equation for B. Oxygen and all combustion products cancel, leaving A converting into B. The enthalpy change is minus three thousand minus minus two thousand nine hundred eighty, giving minus twenty kilojoules per mole. B is therefore lower in enthalpy by twenty kilojoules per mole for the stated phases and conditions. Do not reverse this conclusion because A releases more heat on combustion: its larger release starts from the higher enthalpy state. Enthalpy ordering alone does not establish a Gibbs energy ordering, an equilibrium composition or a reaction rate. Entropy, temperature and activation barriers are separate information. If the combustion data use different water phases or different temperatures, correct those endpoints before subtracting the numbers.
points: A and B: same formula · Same combustion products/phases · Subtract only matched endpoints
ΔcH(A)=−3000; B=−2980 · ΔH(A→B)=−20 kJ/mol · B is lower in enthalpy
H ordering is not G ordering · Entropy and T still matter · No rate or yield follows

chapters.title: Changing product water phase changes combustion enthalpy
chapters.script: A combustion enthalpy is incomplete unless the product states are specified. Producing water vapor leaves the products at a higher enthalpy than producing liquid water at the same temperature. In a supplied methane example, take the combustion enthalpy to carbon dioxide gas and two liquid water molecules as minus eight hundred ninety kilojoules per mole of methane. Use an illustrative water vaporization enthalpy of forty four kilojoules per mole at that same temperature. To change the endpoint to two water vapor molecules, add two vaporization steps, a total of plus eighty eight kilojoules. The gas water combustion enthalpy is therefore minus eight hundred two kilojoules per mole. It remains exothermic but releases less heat in magnitude because the water has not condensed. Reversing the endpoint change requires subtracting those vaporization contributions. The coefficient is the number of water moles produced per written reaction, not the number of hydrogen atoms. These are matched temperature enthalpy corrections, not an instruction to use a boiling point latent heat at an unrelated temperature without adjustment. Always attach the phase labels before comparing fuel energy data.
points: CH4 gives 2 H2O · Liquid-water endpoint:−890 · Units: kJ/mol CH4
At same T: ΔvapH=44 · Add 2×44=88 kJ/mol · Gas-water endpoint:−802
Vapor endpoint has higher H · Less exothermic by88 · Do not mix temperatures

chapters.title: Maximum useful work needs a sign convention and fixed conditions
chapters.formula: At fixed T,p: wnon-PV,on,rev=ΔG; maximum useful work delivered=−ΔG for ΔG<0
chapters.script: Gibbs energy connects a process to a limit on useful work when temperature and pressure are held fixed. Use the chemistry sign convention in which work done on the system is positive. For a reversible process between specified states at fixed temperature and pressure, the nonexpansion work done on the system equals its Gibbs energy change. If that change is minus forty kilojoules, the maximum useful work delivered to the surroundings has positive magnitude forty kilojoules. The work on the system is negative forty; these are two descriptions with opposite sign conventions, not contradictory answers. Pressure volume displacement work is excluded from this useful nonexpansion work limit. Actual irreversible operation delivers less useful work for the same specified overall state change. A device delivering twenty five kilojoules in this example falls below the forty kilojoule limit; it does not violate energy conservation because heat and other energy transfers also enter the full balance. Do not substitute enthalpy for Gibbs energy or use a standard reaction value for an arbitrary nonstandard finite transformation. Identify the actual states, the environmental constraints and whether the requested answer is work on the system or work delivered.
points: Fixed T,p; specified states · Reversible non-PV work on = ΔG · Pressure-volume work excluded

chapters.title: A melting reactant adds a discontinuity to a temperature correction
chapters.script: A reaction enthalpy temperature correction must follow the actual phases. Consider an illustrative one to one conversion of A into B at a fixed pressure. At three hundred kelvin both substances are solids and the reaction enthalpy is twenty kilojoules per mole. A melts at three hundred fifty kelvin with fusion enthalpy five kilojoules per mole, while B remains solid to four hundred kelvin. Use constant molar heat capacities thirty for solid A, fifty for liquid A and forty for solid B, all in joules per mole kelvin. From three hundred to three hundred fifty, products minus reactants gives plus ten joules per mole kelvin, raising the reaction enthalpy by half a kilojoule. Melting raises the reactant enthalpy by five kilojoules, so the reaction enthalpy drops by five, not rises. Above the transition, the heat capacity difference is minus ten, giving another negative half kilojoule. The final reaction enthalpy for liquid A becoming solid B at four hundred kelvin is fifteen kilojoules per mole. A single heat capacity integral that omits fusion cannot connect these endpoints. This supporting piecewise model assumes no other transition or temperature dependence.
points: 300→350 K; both solids · ΔCp=40−30=+10 J/mol K · ΔH:20→20.5 kJ/mol
A melts at350 K · Reactant H rises by5 · Reaction ΔH drops to15.5
350→400 K; A liquid · ΔCp=40−50=−10 · Final ΔH=15 kJ/mol

quiz.question: In the Chemistry convention, expansion work against positive external pressure is:
quiz.explanation: Expansion has positive Delta V, so work on the system w = -P_external Delta V is negative.

quiz.question: A system absorbs 100 J and has 40 J of work done on it. Delta U is:
quiz.explanation: Both incoming transfers are positive: Delta U = q + w = 100 + 40 = 140 J.

quiz.question: For a closed system at constant pressure with only PV work, transferred heat equals:
quiz.explanation: Under these constraints, q_p = Delta H; the constraints are essential to this equality.

quiz.question: Reversing a thermochemical equation changes its Delta H by:
quiz.explanation: Returning between the same endpoint states reverses the enthalpy difference.

quiz.question: Delta H < 0 and Delta S < 0 favour negative Delta G mainly at:
quiz.explanation: The positive -T Delta S contribution grows with temperature and can overcome the negative enthalpy term.

quiz.question: At a given temperature, negative Delta G_standard implies:
options: Every initial mixture has negative actual Delta G
quiz.explanation: Delta G_standard = -RT ln K makes ln K positive, but actual Delta G also depends on Q.

quiz.question: With the supplied methane combustion formation data, products sum to −966 and reactants to −75 kJ/mol. ΔH is:
quiz.explanation: Subtract the reactant sum: −966 − (−75) = −891 kJ/mol.

quiz.question: Lattice dissociation +780 and total hydration −750 kJ/mol give dissolution enthalpy:
quiz.explanation: Add the stated processes with matching endpoints: 780 − 750 = 30.

quiz.question: A combined heat capacity of 500 J/K warms by 2 K. The surroundings absorb:
quiz.explanation: The surroundings gain heat: q = C ΔT = 500 × 2 = +1000 J.

quiz.question: Melting enthalpy 6.00 kJ/mol at equilibrium at 300 K gives entropy change:
quiz.explanation: Use 6000 J/mol divided by 300 K.

quiz.question: Constant molar Cp = 30 J/(mol K), warming from 300 to 600 K, gives ΔS approximately:
At 300 K, ΔH = −6 kJ/mol and ΔSsystem = −10 J/(mol K). ΔG is:
quiz.explanation: Convert entropy to −0.010 kJ/(mol K): −6 − 300(−0.010) = −3.

quiz.question: One mol ideal gas expands reversibly and isothermally from 2 to 4 L at 300 K. With R=8.314 J/(mol K), work on the gas is approximately:
quiz.explanation: Use Chemistry work sign w=−nRT ln(V2/V1); expansion work is negative, and ln2 gives about −1.729 kJ.

quiz.question: For reversible adiabatic compression of a constant-CV ideal monatomic gas from 300 K to half volume, γ=5/3 gives T2 approximately:
quiz.explanation: TV^(γ−1) is constant, so T2=300×2^(2/3). This supporting application requires the reversible ideal-gas assumptions.

quiz.question: With ΔH298=−100 kJ/mol and constant ΔCp=+50 J/(mol K), ΔH398 is:
quiz.explanation: The 100 K increase adds +5000 J/mol=+5 kJ/mol to the supplied reaction enthalpy.

quiz.question: For N2+3H2→2NH3 with supplied S° values 192, 131, 193 J/(mol K), ΔrS° is:
quiz.explanation: Multiply by coefficients before subtracting: 2×193−192−3×131=−199 J/(mol reaction K).

quiz.question: Using that ΔrS°, ΔrH°=−92 kJ/mol and T=298 K gives ΔrG° approximately:
quiz.explanation: Convert −199 J/(mol K) to −0.199 kJ/(mol K), then calculate −92−298×(−0.199).

quiz.question: For 2H2(g)+O2(g)→2H2O(l), given ΔrU=−560 kJ/mol at 300 K and R=0.008314 kJ/(mol K), ΔrH is approximately:
quiz.explanation: Only gases count: Δng=−3. Add −3RT to the supplied internal energy for the written reaction.

quiz.question: For 2H2+O2→2H2O, starting amounts are 0.300 mol H2 and 0.100 mol O2. Maximum reaction extent is:

quiz.question: Two moles melt reversibly at 300 K with ΔHfus=6.00 kJ/mol. System entropy change is:
quiz.explanation: The absorbed heat is 12000 J; reversible transition entropy is 12000/300=40.0 J/K.

quiz.question: For the same reversible melting, total entropy change including a 300 K reservoir is:
quiz.explanation: The reservoir loses the same 12000 J at 300 K, exactly cancelling the system entropy gain.

quiz.question: 1000 J flows from an ideal 400 K reservoir to an ideal 300 K reservoir. Total entropy change is:
quiz.explanation: Add −1000/400 to +1000/300; energy cancels but the entropy contributions have different denominators.

quiz.question: Using −Q/Th+Q/Tc directly requires:
options: Entropy and energy have the same units
Heat must flow cold to hot
quiz.explanation: The fixed-temperature reservoir model permits each entropy change to be written as heat divided by a constant temperature.

Reverse, because actual ΔrG is positive
quiz.explanation: Actual direction follows RT ln(Q/K); the standard-state Gibbs energy alone does not fix direction at the current composition.

quiz.question: At fixed temperature, doubling a reaction with dimensionless K=9 gives the new K:
quiz.explanation: The logarithm of K doubles, hence the equilibrium constant is squared.

quiz.question: Reversing that original reaction with K=9 gives:
quiz.explanation: Reversal changes the sign of standard reaction Gibbs energy and reciprocates K.

quiz.question: One mole ideal gas freely expands into vacuum in a rigid insulated vessel, doubling its available volume. The final equilibrium changes are:

ΔS=0 because no heat crosses the wall

quiz.question: For that ideal-gas free expansion, ΔS for one mole is approximately (R=8.314 J/(mol K)):

quiz.question: One mole monatomic ideal gas has constant Cv=3R/2, doubles T and doubles V. Its entropy change is:
quiz.explanation: Both endpoint contributions matter: Cv ln(T₂/T₁)+R ln(V₂/V₁)=(3R/2+R)ln2.

quiz.question: With R=8.314 J/(mol K), the preceding two-state entropy increase is approximately:

quiz.explanation: ln(K₂/2)=−30000/8.314×(1/330−1/300)=1.09345; exponentiate before multiplying by 2.

quiz.question: For approximately constant negative ΔH°, heating a reaction from T₁ to T₂>T₁ changes its equilibrium constant how?

quiz.question: Matched reaction enthalpies are −57 kJ/mol for H⁺+OH⁻→H₂O and −55 for HA+OH⁻→A⁻+H₂O. The formal HA ionization enthalpy is:
